name: Strong induction
quick: Assume every smaller allowed case to prove the next case.
definition: At target n, the hypothesis provides P(j) for all integers from the domain’s first index through n-1. The target n itself is excluded.
example: To factor n=ab, use the factorization claims at both a and b when $2\leq a,b<n$.
confusion: Smaller indices below the theorem’s first index are not available.

name: Smallest-counterexample argument
quick: Assume a first failure and use the smaller successful cases to contradict it.
definition: Well-ordering supplies a least failing integer in a domain bounded below. Verified bases exclude early failures; the step rules out the alleged first later failure.
example: If a least unrepresentable postage amount n is beyond the bases, representing n-4 may contradict its failure.
confusion: A least member need not exist in an arbitrary nonempty set of real numbers.

name: Prime factorization
quick: Express an integer as a product of primes.
definition: For n at least 2, split a composite n into two smaller factors and factor each recursively. This proves existence of a prime product.
confusion: Existence alone does not show that every factorization has the same primes with the same repetitions.

name: Denomination
quick: The value of one stamp or coin.
definition: A representation uses nonnegative integer counts of the allowed denominations. A zero count of one type is permitted when not forbidden.
confusion: Making one amount does not prove every later amount can be made.

name: Recursive algorithm
quick: A procedure that calls itself on other inputs.
definition: A call runs the procedure for one input and returns its result. To prove correctness, verify both that the calls finish and that their returned values satisfy the specification.
example: A power procedure calls itself at $\lfloor n/2\rfloor$ and combines the returned power.
confusion: An algebraic identity does not establish termination of an implementation.

name: Termination
quick: The computation finishes after finitely many steps.
definition: For recursion, a decreasing nonnegative integer measure can justify termination by induction when base calls finish and each call does only finite remaining work.
example: The call sizes 13,6,3,1,0 strictly decrease and reach a base.
confusion: Repeated halving of a positive real never reaches zero in finitely many exact steps.

name: Well-founded measure
quick: A size whose strict decreases cannot continue forever.
definition: Assign each call a value in a domain with no infinite descending chain. A strictly decreasing nonnegative integer is the standard example here.
example: List length decreases by one when removing its first element.
confusion: A strictly decreasing positive real is not enough.

name: Structural induction
quick: Follow an object’s construction rules to prove its property.
definition: Prove the property for basic objects and show each permitted constructor preserves it when applied to smaller valid objects. An explicit integer size can justify the reasoning for our finite examples.
example: Combining expressions with a and b leaves adds one operation to their $a-1$ and $b-1$ operations.
confusion: Checking only equal-sized splits does not cover every legal construction.

name: Rooted construction tree
quick: A drawing of an object and its parts, starting from one root.
definition: The root represents the whole object; children represent immediate parts. Each non-root node has one parent and child links never lead back to an ancestor. A subtree includes a node and all parts below it.
example: The expression (a+b)*c has a multiplication root, an addition child, and three input leaves.
confusion: This representation records occurrences: repeated labels may appear at different nodes.

name: Leaf and internal node
quick: A leaf has no children; an internal node has children.
definition: In a finite construction tree, leaves are the basic inputs or pieces. Internal nodes record operations combining their children.
example: A board split into lengths 1 and 2 has a root split and two child pieces; splitting the 2 adds another internal node.
confusion: A leaf in a rooted drawing is defined by having no children, not by its visual location.

name: Full binary tree
quick: A rooted tree with exactly two children at every internal node.
definition: It is either one leaf or a root joining two full binary subtrees. Such a finite tree has one more leaf than internal nodes.
example: Joining two leaves makes one internal node and two leaves.
confusion: A node with one child violates the full-binary condition.

name: Tiling
quick: Cover a region completely without gaps or overlapping interiors.
definition: Our domino tilings use rectangles covering two adjacent unit cells, with rotation allowed. A zero-width region has one empty tiling.
example: A 2-by-2 board has two domino tilings: both vertical or both horizontal.
confusion: An empty tiling counts as one completion, not zero choices.

name: Atom occurrence
quick: One appearance of a basic, unsplit object.
definition: An atom is a basic building block; a pair constructor combines two objects. Count each occurrence even if two atoms carry the same label.
example: The pair (a,a) has two atom occurrences, although only one distinct label.
confusion: Counting distinct labels loses repetitions in recursive weight counts.

name: Binary representation
quick: A nonnegative integer expressed using powers of two.
definition: Each power appears at most once in the usual representation, and the empty sum represents zero. Division by 2 recovers the final binary digit and a smaller quotient.
confusion: Existence and uniqueness of a representation require separate arguments.

name: Maximum
quick: $\max$ selects the greatest value in the specified collection.
definition: For a finite nonempty real collection, its maximum is a member at least as large as every other member. State the collection being compared.
confusion: Do not take a maximum of an empty collection without a stated convention.
